record.context_brief: Complexity of core coding optimization problems
record.original_question: What is the computational complexity of determining A(n, d), A(n, d, w), k[n, d], and the analogous optimization problems for permutation codes described in the paper?

evidence.quote: Open Question 3.4. What is the complexity status of computing A(n, d), A(n, d, w), k[n, d] and the above permutation analogues?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
For a positive integer n and integer d with 1 ≤ d ≤ n, let A(n, d) denote the maximum size of a binary code of length n with minimum Hamming distance at least d, i.e., the largest cardinality of a subset C ⊆ {0,1}^n such that any two distinct codewords differ in at least d coordinates. For an integer w with 0 ≤ w ≤ n, let A(n, d, w) denote the maximum size of a binary constant-weight code of length n, minimum Hamming distance at least d, with every codeword having Hamming weight exactly w. For positive integers n and d, let k[n, d] denote the maximum dimension k of a binary linear code of length n with minimum distance at least d (so that 2^{k[n,d]} is the largest size of a linear code attaining these parameters). For the permutation analogue, equip the symmetric group S_n with the Hamming metric d_H(σ, τ) = |{i : σ(i) ≠ τ(i)}|, and let M(n, d) denote the maximum size of a subset Γ ⊆ S_n such that d_H(σ, τ) ≥ d for all distinct σ, τ ∈ Γ.

The input to each problem is the parameters (n, d), (n, d, w), or (n, d), encoded in binary (so the input size is logarithmic in n). Determine the computational complexity of each of the following decision/optimization problems:
(i) Given (n, d, N), decide whether A(n, d) ≥ N (equivalently, compute A(n, d)).
(ii) Given (n, d, w, N), decide whether A(n, d, w) ≥ N (equivalently, compute A(n, d, w)).
(iii) Given (n, d, k), decide whether k[n, d] ≥ k (equivalently, compute k[n, d]).
(iv) Given (n, d, N), decide whether M(n, d) ≥ N, and the analogous constant-weight and linear-style problems for permutation codes.

In particular, determine whether each of these problems is in P, NP-complete, coNP-hard, or otherwise classify them within the standard complexity hierarchy.
artifact.status_search_result: No source was found establishing the computational complexity of computing A(n,d), A(n,d,w), k[n,d], or their permutation-code analogues. While related problems such as minimum-distance decoding and computing the minimum distance of a linear/stabilizer code are known to be NP-hard, the complexity of these maximum-size code-parameter problems (with parameters given in binary) appears to remain unresolved in the literature.

status_evidence.title: Computational methods in coding theory
status_evidence.snippet: A(n,d) denotes the maximum size of a binary code of length n and minimum Hamming distance d, and determining A(n,d) is one of the most fundamental subjects in coding theory.
status_evidence.claim: Determining A(n,d) is a fundamental and longstanding problem in coding theory; exact values are known only in a limited range.

status_evidence.title: New Bounds on the Size of Binary Codes with Large Minimum Distance
status_evidence.snippet: New bounds on A(n,d) for binary codes are still being derived, with values for many (n,d) parameter pairs not exactly known.
status_evidence.claim: A(n,d) is unknown for many parameters, and recent work focuses on improved bounds rather than exact computation.

status_evidence.title: Strengthened semidefinite programming bounds for codes
status_evidence.snippet: Semidefinite programming bounds give upper bounds on A(n,d) computable in polynomial time at each level.
status_evidence.claim: Only bounds, not exact computation, are known to be tractable; the exact complexity of computing A(n,d) is not established.
